\begin{abstract}
The final project is a small research study in natural language processing. Choose one question, build a baseline, and test a targeted change under a fixed budget. The deliverables are a poster presentation, a research report, and reproducibility materials. This guide merges the project briefs and the Lecture 8 topics into eight tracks (A--H, 79 briefs), ordered from the most popular and easiest to grasp to the more specialised, with competitions and entrepreneurship last. The same content, with media, inspiration posts and a Chinese version, is on the course website: \url{https://nlp-course-cuhksz.github.io/final-project.html}. This guide covers CSC5051, CSC6052, and MDS5110. Version of November 9, 2026.
\end{abstract}

\section{The question, and eight tracks that answer it}
One question organises every project this term: \emph{with today's AI tools, what LLM research can a team of two or three finish in four weeks and write up as a research report?} You choose one question, build a working baseline, and test \textbf{one targeted change} under a fixed budget. What is graded is not the size of the system but the clarity of the question, the fairness of the comparison, and the honesty of the write-up: a project that shows one clean success and one well-explained failure is a good project.

AI coding tools have changed what a four-week project can be. A team can now stand up a 3D scene, a game, a training run, a dataset pipeline or an agent harness in days instead of weeks. We therefore ask every team the same thing: \emph{what can you learn in a month that you could not learn without doing the experiment?} Tracks are entry points, not fences: a campus NPC project is Track C but borrows memory designs from Track A and evaluation discipline from Track D.

Every brief in the appendices states what to compare, what to measure, what to deliver, and a four-week plan. Compute tags: \emph{API} means a hosted or small local model is enough; \emph{1 GPU} means a single 16--24 GB GPU for hours; \emph{multi-GPU} means several GPUs for days. Posts from X cited as inspiration on the website were located through search and could not all be opened directly; treat them as design prompts.

\paragraph{Where the briefs come from.}
Each track starts from published work that a team can extend in four weeks; the appendices cite it brief by brief and link to code and data. Track~A builds on executable agent benchmarks such as SWE-bench~\citep{jimenez2023swe} and MLE-bench~\citep{chan2024mle}, and on agents that write surveys~\citep{wang2024autosurvey}. Track~B asks for small, testable changes to post-training in the spirit of selective token training~\citep{lin2024rho}, reinforcement learning on high-entropy tokens~\citep{wang20258020} and simplified policy optimisation~\citep{yu2025dapo,liu2025understanding}. Track~C draws on generative agents~\citep{park2023generative}, egocentric assistants~\citep{yang2025egolife}, embodied question answering~\citep{majumdar2024openeqa}, and courses and lecture videos generated by AI~\citep{yu2024mooc,zhu2025paper2video}. Track~D builds on rubric-based evaluation~\citep{arora2025healthbench}, long multimodal context~\citep{wang2024longllava,song2024milebench} and audits of which model an API really serves~\citep{gao2024model,zhang2026real}. Track~E follows audits such as that of \citet{hofmann2024dialect}; Track~F starts from speculative decoding and the alignment of a draft model with its target~\citep{li2025eagle,zhou2023distillspec}, and from engines that stream a trillion-parameter mixture of experts from disk on a single CPU~\citep{khan2026kimik3c}; Track~H from open tutoring systems~\citep{zhao2026deeptutor} and the evidence that unguarded AI help can harm learning~\citep{bastani2025guardrails}.

\paragraph{New in this version (November 9).}
An ML-engineering agent that enters a Kaggle competition on its own (A11); post-training variants of your own instead of a reproduction (B6); a visual personal assistant (C4); a clearer active embodied QA brief (C6); an AI lecture series with generated courseware, TTS narration and a recurring host (C20); multimodal long context with LongLLaVA (D1); bonus questions on identifying the model behind a relay API (D3), on aligning a draft model with different targets (F5), and on running a 2.78-trillion-parameter mixture of experts in 8~GB of RAM (F6); and DeepTutor as a starting point for the AI tutor (H1).

\paragraph{Use strong models, and say so.}
We encourage you to use the strongest model you can access as a planner, coder, judge or research assistant: an API model such as \href{https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5}{Claude Opus 5.5}, or a strong open-weight model such as \href{https://github.com/zai-org/GLM-5}{GLM-5.x} or \href{https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3-VL}{Qwen3-VL} served locally. Log the model version and its role in every experiment. Where a model writes code or judges outputs, verify with executable tests, ground truth, or a human audit of a sample. For hosted competitions, use only the models and tools the organizer allows. The report must describe material uses of generative AI in coding, data, evaluation and writing.

\paragraph{How to choose a topic (from Lecture 8).}
Combine your expertise with AI: a previous major in mathematics, science, engineering, medicine, law or finance is an advantage. Combine your background: if your native language or dialect is under-represented, train or audit a model for it; local culture and heritage count (黄梅戏, 甲骨文, 京剧, 中医, 相声). Start from a real need near you: a relative with diabetes who needs out-of-hospital management, a friend with a visual impairment, a family shop that needs a seller agent. Your interest matters most: pick the question you would read about on a Sunday.

A suggested four-week research window runs from November 13 to December 11. Week 1: freeze the task, the held-out split, a working baseline and the primary metric. Week 2: build the one change you are testing and smoke-test it end to end. Week 3: matched-budget runs, seeds, ablation and error analysis. Week 4: reproduce the key result from a clean clone and prepare the demo or result figure. Keep a smaller fallback experiment ready from week 1, so a failed main change still yields a result. Rule of thumb: if the baseline is not running by the end of week 1, shrink the task, not the comparison.

\section{Teams and topic selection}
You may work alone or in a team; the suggested size is two or three. A larger team must explain how the workload and individual responsibilities justify it. Each student is assessed individually, and the report carries a contribution statement. If you collaborate with people outside the course, identify your own work.

The optional one-page proposal is worth writing whenever the research question, evaluation method or compute budget needs early feedback. State the question and motivation, the closest prior work, the data or environment, the baseline, the proposed change, the primary metric, the resource budget, and a smaller fallback experiment. Submit it through the channel announced by the teaching team.

\section{Experiment design}
Begin with one working baseline and one measurable outcome. Compare your method on the same held-out tasks and report the variables that affect interpretation: model version, prompts, training tokens, time limits, hardware, API spend. Include at least one comparison that isolates the main change, and show both a success and a failure with your explanation. A table of three numbers with seeds and a replay script is worth more than a page of screenshots.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{One change.} Everything else fixed: model, prompts, data, budget, seeds, evaluation code.
\item \textbf{Matched budget.} Same number of calls, tokens, simulator evaluations or training tokens per condition; wall-clock reported separately.
\item \textbf{Held-out.} A split (or scenarios, rooms, prompts, briefs) that nobody tuned on; frozen in week 1.
\item \textbf{Independent checker.} Executable tests, simulator state, ground truth, or a different model validated against a human-audited sample.
\item \textbf{Seeds and variance.} At least two seeds for anything stochastic; report the spread.
\item \textbf{Negative result kept.} If the change does not help, the error analysis is the contribution.
\item \textbf{Replayable.} Traces, logs and configs in the repository; one command reproduces the headline number.
\end{itemize}

\section{Deliverables and assessment}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Poster and presentation (10 points).} State the question, baseline, main result, and one limitation. A live demo or recorded replay can illustrate the result. Use the \href{https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1pBJuB-wazGyGHTiDNQ6msihS2cyyZDYL71VgE6o3FrE/edit}{sample poster template}; past posters are collected at \url{https://nlp-course-cuhksz.github.io/writing-tips.html}.
\item \textbf{Final report (45 points).} Submit a PDF of at most six pages of main text using the \href{https://www.overleaf.com/read/nkgjmyqghssh\#3c4f20}{course report template}: motivation, related work, method, evaluation, results, failures and limitations, plus a contribution statement and a generative-AI use statement. Read the Lecture 8 writing tips first (a good paper reads like a smooth film, with no dull stretch).
\item \textbf{Reproducibility.} Code on GitHub with a README, environment and model versions, evaluation inputs or instructions for obtaining them, and the commands to reproduce the main result. Competition entries add the dated score or submission link.
\end{itemize}

Reports are made public after the poster session unless you notify the teaching team. If you release your work after the course, please acknowledge the course.

\paragraph{Example contribution statement.}
Alice designed the evaluation and annotated the held-out cases. Bob implemented the baseline and the proposed method. Both ran experiments and wrote the report.

\paragraph{Proposal template (optional, one page, due November 13).}
Title; team (names, student IDs, course codes); track and brief (e.g., Track A, brief A2) or custom. (1) Question and motivation: what will we know at the end that we do not know now? (2) Closest prior work and what we do differently. (3) Data, environment or benchmark, and the held-out split frozen in week 1. (4) Baseline: what, from where, expected number. (5) The one change we test. (6) Primary metric, plus one cost metric. (7) Resource budget: compute, API spend, data access, accounts. (8) Four-week plan. (9) Fallback experiment. (10) Risks and what we need from the teaching team.

\paragraph{FAQ.}
\emph{Do we need a GPU?} Not for most briefs in Tracks A, C, D, E, G and H, which run on an API model plus a laptop. Tracks B and F assume at least one GPU; Kaggle and Colab are enough for the small-scale version. \emph{Can we propose something not in this guide?} Yes: use the proposal template, name the closest track, and make sure there is a baseline, a held-out split and one change to test. \emph{Is a position paper (Track E) a final project?} Yes, if it contains a falsifiable claim and at least one measurement you ran. \emph{Can a startup prototype (Track H) be our project?} Yes, as a product experiment with two variants, a metric fixed in advance, real users, a cost table and a business memo. \emph{What if the main change does not work?} Report it: a clean negative result with an error analysis and a working fallback experiment is a complete project.
